title: Vegetables in the Philippines: What to Grow, When, and How to Feed Them
metaTitle: Vegetables in the Philippines: Crops, Fertilizer, Pests
metaDescription: Vegetables in the Philippines: what grows in the lowlands and in Benguet, the best fertilizer for vegetables, tomato feeding, and the pests to watch for.
excerpt: Vegetables in the Philippines come from two very different farms. In the lowlands it is the gulayan of ampalaya, sitaw, talong, okra, kalabasa, pechay, kangkong and tomato. Up in Benguet it is the cool terraces that send cabbage, carrots and potatoes to Manila. This guide covers what to plant, when to plant it, how to feed each crop, and which pests take the most harvest.

blocks.text:
Many farmers grow gulay (vegetables) on a small lot next to their palay or mais, because pechay can be sold five to seven weeks after sowing. But vegetables also punish mistakes quickly. A week of heavy rain on ripening tomatoes can wipe out much of the harvest.

The rates below come from Department of Agriculture (DA) and Agricultural Training Institute (ATI) guides for fields without a soil test. So when you can, have your soil analyzed at the provincial soils laboratory.
The main vegetables in the Philippines
Lowland vegetables

In the lowlands the common crops are the pinakbet and sinigang vegetables: ampalaya (bitter gourd), sitaw (string beans), talong (eggplant), okra, kalabasa (squash), pechay, kangkong and tomato. Most want full sun and well drained loam rich in organic matter.

blocks.caption: When common lowland vegetables give their first harvest, from DA and ATI guides
rows: 30 to 90 days after planting, then regrowth
Flowers 40 to 75 days after planting, pods 4 to 6 days after flowering
Varies by variety, so check the seed pack

blocks.text: Highland vegetables of Benguet

In the Cordillera the cool air lets farmers grow crops that struggle in lowland heat. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reports the Cordillera as the country's top producer of cabbage, carrots and potatoes, and Benguet is its largest producing province. Much of that harvest passes through the La Trinidad trading post.

A Benguet State University survey of about 100 farmers per crop put average yields at 22 tons of cabbage, 20 tons of carrots and 16 tons of potatoes per hectare. It also found that fertilizer and soil amendments make up 23 percent of the cost of growing cabbage.
When to plant

The calendar follows the rain. The DA tomato guide for Cagayan Valley plants tomatoes from November to February in the lowlands and from September to January in hilly areas. Ampalaya can go in any time, but it does best from October to February.

Off season planting, May to September for tomato, pays more because prices climb when supply drops. But wet season fields need raised ground and good drainage. Typhoons are the other risk, so stagger your plantings instead of betting one lot on one month.

For your own town, the anee.io [When to Plant Analysis](/features/when-to-plant-analysis) reads the local weather first, and the forecast for each lot tells you when to hold a spray.
Best fertilizer for vegetables

There is no single best fertilizer for vegetables. The pattern in DA guides is the same for most crops. First, build the soil with organic matter. Next, give a complete fertilizer at planting. Then side dress with nitrogen and potash while the crop grows.
Organic base: compost and chicken dung

The DA vegetable guides start with organic fertilizer. The ampalaya guide asks for 10 to 20 tons of compost or decomposed manure per hectare before field preparation. In the Cordillera, the DA organic guide uses 2 to 4 kilograms of compost per square meter of plot.

Chicken dung as fertilizer is popular because it is cheap and rich. The ATI pechay guide for Central Visayas puts one sack of chicken dung, one kilo of complete fertilizer and four kilos of urea on every 20 meter bed. For talong, an eggplant leaflet credited to ATI uses 0.5 kilograms of decomposed chicken manure with 0.4 kilograms of 16 20 0 per 10 meters of furrow. We saw that rate only in reprints, so confirm it with your agriculture office.

Use only well rotted dung. The DA Bicol organic guide explains that raw organic matter releases acids and ties up nitrogen while it decays, so young plants turn yellow. Some farms go fully natural. Visitor accounts describe Palaya Natural Farm in Tanay, Rizal, better known for its dragon fruit, as growing vegetables with organic methods, which we could not confirm officially. For more options, see our [organic fertilizer examples](/blog/organic-fertilizer-examples).
Complete fertilizer: triple 14 and 16 16 16

Fertilizer 14 14 14, which many farmers call triple 14 fertilizer, carries 14 percent each of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. It is the standard basal fertilizer for vegetables in DA guides. For example, ampalaya gets 20 grams, about two tablespoons, per hill, while tomato gets one tablespoon per plant.

Some dealers also stock fertilizer 16 16 16. It does the same job with a little more of each nutrient per bag, so use slightly less. Our guide to [complete fertilizer 14 14 14](/blog/complete-fertilizer-14-14-14) shows the bag math.

The 16 20 fertilizer, sold as 16 20 0 ammonium phosphate, has no potash but more phosphorus for young roots. Some eggplant guides use it as a basal fertilizer, and a soil test tells you whether the potassium is already enough. See our [16 20 0 fertilizer](/blog/16-20-0-fertilizer) guide.
Side dress with urea and potash

After planting, vegetables need nitrogen for leaves and potassium for fruit. The DA ampalaya guide side dresses 10 grams of urea, about one tablespoon, per hill three to four weeks after planting. After that it repeats the dose every two weeks for two or three more rounds. Cover each dose with fine soil so the urea does not escape into the air.
Foliar fertilizer spray

A foliar fertilizer spray feeds the plant through its leaves. Treat it as a supplement to soil feeding, because leaves take in only small amounts at a time. Organic growers often use fish amino acid: ATI Cordillera mixes 2 tablespoons in 1 liter of water and sprays every 7 days, from new seedlings until fruiting.

For a commercial foliar fertilizer, follow the label. More in our [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer) guide.
Fertilizer for tomato plants
Here is a simple tomato program for fields without a soil test, combining the DA and ATI guides.

blocks.caption: Fertilizer for tomato plants without a soil test, from the DA Cagayan Valley and ATI Cordillera tomato guides
rows: Decomposed animal manure or commercial organic fertilizer
Complete fertilizer 14 14 14 in the hole, covered with compost
Urea (46 0 0) and muriate of potash (0 0 60), buried 1 inch deep and 3 to 4 inches from the stem
Urea and muriate of potash, same method

blocks.text:
During flowering and fruit set, ATI also suggests calcium sprays made from eggshells. Water only to keep the root zone moist, because tomato is very sensitive to flooding and excess moisture brings blight.

In anee.io, each dose becomes a dated task on the [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), counted from each lot's transplanting day. On Solo Farmer and Farm Owner, the [inventory](/features/farm-inventory-and-expenses) then takes the urea and potash off your stock as each activity uses them.
Common pests and diseases
Thrips

Thrips are tiny insects that rasp leaves and suck the sap, leaving silvery scars that turn brown. Melon thrips (Thrips palmi) attack ampalaya, melons, talong and tomato. Check the undersides of young leaves and the flowers, then see our page on [thrips](/pests/thrips).
Aphids

Aphids are soft green or black insects that cluster on shoots and under leaves, curling them and spreading viruses. Two common aphids cause much of the damage, and their scientific names help when you read DA bulletins and pesticide labels. The cotton or melon aphid, Aphis gossypii, feeds on talong, okra, sili and gourds. The green peach aphid, Myzus persicae, prefers pechay, cabbage and potato. See our page on [mites and aphids](/pests/hanip-mites-and-aphids).
Cutworms

Cutworms are moth larvae that hide in the soil by day and feed at night, often cutting seedlings at the soil line. The common cutworm, Spodoptera litura, also strips pechay and cabbage leaves. The DA Bicol guide says to handpick them, spray botanicals and net the seedlings. More on our [cutworm](/pests/cutworm) page.
Anthracnose

Anthracnose is a fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum. It makes sunken, dark spots on fruit and leaves, and it spreads fastest in warm, wet weather. The DA lists it among the prevalent diseases of tomato, and it also hits sili and ampalaya. Plant tolerant varieties where you can, remove infected fruit, and read our [anthracnose](/diseases/anthracnose) page for the fungicide groups used against it.

blocks.title: Spray only what the label allows
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority) for your crop. Follow the label rate and the waiting days before harvest, which matter most on leafy vegetables.

items.q: What are the most common vegetables in the Philippines?
items.a: In the lowlands: ampalaya, sitaw, talong, okra, kalabasa, pechay, kangkong and tomato. In the highlands, the Cordillera leads in cabbage, carrots and potatoes, with Benguet its largest producer.

items.q: What is the best fertilizer for vegetables?
items.a: Decomposed compost or chicken dung before planting, complete fertilizer 14 14 14 at planting, then urea and muriate of potash as side dress.
Not better, just a little stronger per bag. Both carry equal nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, so use slightly less 16 16 16.

items.q: How often should I spray foliar fertilizer?
items.a: Follow the label for a commercial product. For homemade fish amino acid, ATI Cordillera uses 2 tablespoons per liter of water once a week.
